name: Laser comb
lead: A laser comb is a handheld hair-growth device with a row of teeth that part the hair while low-power red laser light is directed at the scalp. It applies the technique known as low-level laser therapy (LLLT) or photobiomodulation, and is marketed for androgenetic alopecia (pattern hair loss). The best-known model, the HairMax LaserComb, has been described in the dermatology literature as FDA-cleared for this indication [3][5].

Users move the comb across the thinning areas of the scalp several times a week. Compared with laser caps and helmets, which cover the whole scalp at once, the comb requires manual sweeping, so exposure depends on how thoroughly the user covers each region. Combs generally cost less than caps.

Published randomized, sham-controlled trials of laser combs report greater increases in terminal hair density than sham devices, and systematic reviews of LLLT in general have reached broadly favourable but cautious conclusions [5][6]. Medical reviews place laser devices behind minoxidil and finasteride as treatments, with some recommending the FDA-cleared comb as a follow-on option for people who respond poorly to the drugs [4]. The same body of research has not established the optimal dose, schedule or long-term outcomes.

paras: A laser comb contains one or more laser diodes whose beams are split so that each tooth of the comb emits light. The teeth are intended to move hair aside so that light reaches the scalp surface. In the 2009 pivotal trial, the HairMax LaserComb was described as a hand-held Class 3R device using a single laser module that produces nine beams at a wavelength of 655 nm [7]. Later trials tested combs with 7, 9 and 12 beams [8].

Laser combs belong to the wider family of light-based hair devices that also includes laser caps, helmets and LED panels. Reviews note that low-level lasers and LEDs have been used under the names low-level laser therapy, cold laser therapy, red light therapy and photobiomodulation [1].

The biological effect of low-power laser light on hair is usually traced to the Hungarian physician Endre Mester. According to Wikipedia, he was trying to replicate a mouse tumour experiment with a ruby laser that turned out to be weaker than intended; the treated mice regrew shaved hair faster than controls, and he published the observation in 1967 [1]. Mester called the approach laser biostimulation, and his work was later carried to the United States by his sons [1].

Home laser combs for hair loss emerged from this lineage. A 2013 review for primary-care practitioners treated the FDA-cleared HairMax LaserComb as an option behind first-line drugs [4], and the 2009 multicentre trial of that device is among the earlier published controlled studies of a comb-format device [7].

The generally accepted explanation for photobiomodulation is that cells absorb red or near-infrared light through the mitochondrial enzyme cytochrome c oxidase, altering cellular energy metabolism [1][2]. Proponents of laser hair therapy propose that this stimulates follicle cells, lengthens the growth (anagen) phase and reduces inflammation. Reviews describe these mechanisms as hypotheses and note that the dose range matters, since light delivered below the effective range does not appear to be beneficial [1].

Animal studies are consistent with a hair effect but are not direct evidence of human benefit. A laser comb accelerated hair regrowth in a rat model of chemotherapy-induced alopecia [12], and a comb device was reported to alleviate symptoms in a mouse model of alopecia areata, a different autoimmune condition [11].

The 2009 multicentre trial randomized men with androgenetic alopecia 2:1 to the HairMax LaserComb or a sham device for 26 weeks. Among 110 completers, the active group showed a significantly larger increase in terminal hair density, and self-assessed regrowth also favoured the comb. No serious adverse events were reported and adverse effects did not differ significantly from sham [7].

A 2014 report pooled four randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trials of laser combs in men and women (269 randomized in total). Mean terminal hair count increased by about 18 to 26 hairs per square centimetre at 26 weeks in the active arms, compared with roughly 2 to 9 in the sham arms, with whole-scalp treatment three times weekly. No serious adverse events were reported in any subject using the comb [8].

A 2017 systematic review of LLLT for androgenetic alopecia evaluated eleven studies covering 680 patients. Nine of the eleven studies measuring hair count or density found significant improvement in men and women, and patient satisfaction was reported as positive though less pronounced than the objective outcomes [5]. A 2022 Bayesian network meta-analysis of placebo-controlled trials with at least 20 participants included low-level laser comb treatment among its comparators; in women, it estimated a gain of about 16.6 terminal hairs per square centimetre at 24 weeks, compared with about 12.1 for 2% minoxidil in the same analysis [6]. A 2017 meta-analysis in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology found low-level laser therapy in men to be superior to placebo [3].

Other reviews have examined LLLT as monotherapy or concomitant therapy in both sexes [13]. Combination use has also been tested. In a randomized trial of 50 patients in Iran, adding low-level light from a laser comb to 5% minoxidil produced significantly higher hair density, diameter and satisfaction than minoxidil combined with a switched-off device [9].

Wikipedia summarises the review history more cautiously: an earlier 2012 review found little evidence for lasers in hair loss, and 2014 reviews described tentative or mixed evidence with high risk of bias, while a 2017 review reported that most trials showed improvement over baseline or control [1]. Reviewers consistently call for larger, longer, independently funded randomized trials [1][10].

In the trials above, serious adverse events were not reported with the comb, and side-effect rates did not differ significantly from sham devices [7][8]. Wikipedia notes occasional reports of mild pain or skin irritation after red-light therapy, that long-term effects on skin and hair are unknown, and that eye protection is suggested for some devices [1]. Reviews of laser-based hair treatments describe them as affordable, user-friendly and generally safe while calling for more data [10].

Laser combs are discussed on hair-loss forums alongside laser caps, minoxidil and finasteride. Threads in the archived r/tressless community and on Hair Loss Talk ask whether users have had positive results from laser devices, and share individual experience reports [14][15][16]. Participants commonly compare combs with caps in terms of price and the effort of sweeping the scalp manually, a point that follows from the design differences described above.
Clinical reviews and community discussion both tend to place light therapy as an add-on rather than a replacement for drug treatments [4].

In the United States, low-level laser devices for hair growth are regulated as medical devices and have been cleared by the FDA as Class II devices [2]. Wikipedia suggests using only devices certified by the FDA for dermatologic application [1]; Grokipedia likewise describes such devices as Class II devices cleared via 510(k) [2]. The FDA's separate 2014-2015 action against a different laser maker, QLaser, concerned unsupported claims to treat hundreds of diseases and is unrelated to hair combs [1].

timeline.event: Endre Mester publishes the observation that low-power ruby laser light speeds hair regrowth in mice [1].
Multicentre sham-controlled trial of the HairMax LaserComb in men with androgenetic alopecia published [7].
Pooled report of four sham-controlled laser comb trials in men and women published [8].
Systematic reviews of LLLT for androgenetic alopecia report mostly positive but limited evidence [3][5].
Randomized trial of laser comb light added to minoxidil published [9].
Network meta-analysis includes laser comb treatment among hair-regrowth therapies [6].

lore.intro: On hair-loss forums the laser comb is discussed as a cheaper, hands-on alternative to a laser cap, usually as an add-on to drug treatments. Archived threads show users asking for and sharing personal results [14][15][16].

claims.claim: Laser combs regrow or thicken hair in androgenetic alopecia
claims.believers: Users in hair-loss threads ask for and post personal accounts of laser use, with some describing it as part of their regimen [14][15][16].
claims.experts: Sham-controlled trials report greater terminal hair counts with laser combs than with sham devices, and a systematic review found significant improvement in nine of eleven studies, but samples are small, follow-up is short and industry ties are common [5][7][8].

claims.claim: A comb gives the same benefit as a laser cap but needs more effort
claims.believers: Forum participants discuss combs and caps as interchangeable options and weigh the lower price of a comb against the manual coverage it requires [15].
claims.experts: A review noted that device type (hat, comb or helmet) and treatment duration did not appear to alter effectiveness, though this is drawn from heterogeneous trials rather than head-to-head comparison [1].

claims.claim: Laser therapy is a useful add-on to minoxidil or finasteride
claims.believers: Community members commonly describe light therapy as one layer of a combined routine alongside drugs [14].
claims.experts: A randomized trial found more hair density when comb light therapy was added to 5% minoxidil than minoxidil alone, and a primary-care review placed the FDA-cleared comb after first-line drugs [4][9].
